definition: Opulent means characterized by rich abundance verging on ostentation.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word opulent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know opulent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The wedding tent was opulent beyond anything the invitation hinted: silk carpets over the grass, towers of peonies, and waiters pouring from gold pitchers.
Comfortable stops short of opulent — comfort asks only that nothing pinch; it makes no show of wealth at all.
Plush stops short of opulent — a plush seat pampers you quietly, while an opulent room performs its riches for everyone in it.

Sumptuous means rich and costly in the materials themselves — velvet, marble, aged silk — luxury you can touch and taste. Opulent adds performance: the abundance is arranged to be noticed, wealth staged for an audience. Sumptuous needs no spectators at all; opulent exists to be seen.

Lavish praises the spending — a lavish party, lavish gifts — generosity poured out without counting the cost. Opulent describes the resulting look: massed wealth on display, rooms and feasts performing their riches. A host is lavish in what they pour out; the ballroom they fill is opulent.
stripped to the bare essentials on purpose
without decoration of any kind

Opulent means characterized by rich abundance verging on ostentation.
The sultan's guest suite stopped conversation: carpets six layers deep, perfumed fountains, pomegranates stacked in silver towers — an opulent display meant to say the household had wealth to waste.
Opulent goes beyond 'luxurious' — luxury can be quiet, but opulence performs: the abundance is arranged to be seen, rich to the point of showing off.

Opulent can flatter or needle, and this unit's neighbors mark its edges: lavish (in the reference list) praises generous spending, while opulent describes the look of massed wealth — and can hint at showing off.
If the riches tip into tastelessness outright, English reaches past opulent to gaudy.

When the Alhambra Theater reopened after its restoration, ticket holders came early just to stand in the lobby.
The architects had returned the building to its 1920s self: gold-leafed ceilings, mirrored staircases, velvet swags in three shades of red.
Critics called the effect opulent, and the theater's own marketing leaned into the word, promising an evening of borrowed splendor to anyone with a ticket.
Historians note that the original owners designed the lobby precisely so that every dollar spent would be visible to arriving crowds.
The auditorium seats, by contrast, were left plain -- the show of wealth was always meant for the entrance, where everyone could see it.
